strategy_title: Persistent Tile Loop Hurts When Register Pressure Rises
strategy_description: Wrapping a pointwise kernel body in a persistent strided tile loop (grid=num_SMs, loop over tiles) increased register usage from 28 to 40 registers/thread. This reduced theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% (Block Limit Registers dropped from 16 to 12 blocks/SM) and achieved occupancy from 24% to 11.6%, causing duration to increase from 3.1 µs to 4.26 µs. The persistent loop added loop-control overhead and register pressure that more than offset any wave-boundary savings, especially when the original grid was already small enough that the loop body executed only a handful of iterations per SM.
slow_pseudocode:
# Persistent loop version (SLOWER)
@triton.jit
def kernel(ptrs..., xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    num_programs = tl.num_programs(0)
    num_tiles = tl.cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK)
    for tile_id in tl.range(pid, num_tiles, num_programs):
        xoffset = tile_id * XBLOCK
        xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
        xmask = xindex < xnumel
        # ... loads, compute, store ...
# grid = (132,)  # one CTA per SM
fast_pseudocode:
# One-CTA-per-tile version (FASTER for this workload)
@triton.jit
def kernel(ptrs..., xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xnumel = 94080
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    # ... loads, compute, store ...
# grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK),)  # up to 735 CTAs
applicable_when: Persistent tile scheduling helps when: (1) the kernel has many tiles per SM (waves_per_sm >> 1 with the persistent grid), (2) register pressure is already low (registers_per_thread << 32) so the loop overhead does not push past a register-limited occupancy cliff, and (3) the kernel body is compute-heavy enough to amortize loop control overhead.
do_not_apply_when: Do NOT apply persistent tile scheduling when: (1) the kernel is already register-heavy (registers_per_thread >= 28) and adding loop variables will cross a register-file occupancy boundary (e.g., from 100% to 75% theoretical occupancy); (2) the total tile count is small (< 5 tiles per SM) so the loop adds overhead without meaningful wave-boundary savings; (3) the kernel is a short-duration pointwise op (< 5 µs) where launch overhead and register pressure dominate over wave-boundary idle time.
framework_notes: In Triton, using tl.range() inside a @triton.jit kernel for a persistent loop increases register pressure because loop induction variables and tile-local temporaries must all live in registers simultaneously. The autotune configs also lost num_stages, which may have further reduced instruction-level parallelism.

strategy_title: Persistent Tile Loop Hurts When Register Pressure Rises
strategy_description: Adding a persistent while-loop inside a Triton kernel to reduce grid size increased register usage from 28 to 38 registers/thread, which dropped theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% (Block Limit Registers fell from 16 to 12 blocks/SM). The reduced occupancy caused achieved occupancy to fall from 24% to 13%, warp cycles per issued instruction to nearly double (10.89→19.96), and eligible warps per scheduler to collapse from 0.66 to 0.13, resulting in a 33% slowdown despite the grid being slightly better utilized. The persistent loop pattern is counterproductive when the kernel is already register-heavy: the loop control variables and tile_id bookkeeping consume additional registers that spill the kernel past a register-limit occupancy boundary.
slow_pseudocode:
# Before: single-pass, 28 registers/thread, 100% theoretical occupancy
@triton.jit
def kernel(in_out_ptr0, ..., xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    # ... compute and store
    tl.store(in_out_ptr0 + xindex, result, xmask)
fast_pseudocode:
# After (SLOWER): persistent loop, 38 registers/thread, 75% theoretical occupancy
@triton.jit
def kernel(in_out_ptr0, ..., xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    num_programs = tl.num_programs(0)
    tile_id = pid
    while tile_id * XBLOCK < xnumel:  # <-- loop adds register pressure
        xoffset = tile_id * XBLOCK
        xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
        xmask = xindex < xnumel
        # ... compute and store
        tl.store(in_out_ptr0 + xindex, result, xmask)
        tile_id += num_programs  # <-- extra register consumed
applicable_when: Kernel has very low register usage (≤24 registers/thread) with significant headroom before hitting a register-limit occupancy boundary; grid is severely under-saturating SMs (waves_per_sm < 0.5) and the bottleneck is confirmed to be occupancy rather than memory bandwidth.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel already uses ≥28 registers/thread and is near a register-limit occupancy boundary (Block Limit Registers close to Block Limit Warps); adding loop control variables will push register count past the next boundary, reducing theoretical occupancy and worsening achieved occupancy and warp scheduling. Also avoid when the kernel is already memory-bandwidth bound rather than latency-bound.
framework_notes: In Triton, the persistent loop pattern uses tl.num_programs(0) to get the actual grid size at runtime. The while-loop condition (tile_id * XBLOCK < xnumel) and the stride (tile_id += num_programs) each consume registers. Removing num_stages from autotune configs (as done here) may also affect pipeline depth and contribute to the regression independently of the persistent loop.
